title: EARLY WARNING SIGNS AND SHOCK EMERGENCIES
knowledge: Explain the rationale for EARLY WARNING SIGNS i.e. to provide an integrated approach to the recognition and response to 'at risk' patients, preventing avoidable deterioration.
Explore how being aware of EARLY WARNING SIGNS will improve patient outcomes and why this is important in terms of the quality of life.
Explain why real time vital signs are important when a patient is recognized as 'at risk' e.g. initial baseline and on-going trends.
Discuss the EARLY WARNING SIGNS Tool developed for area of practice and explain how the EWS Scale works.

List the NURSING INTERVENTIONS AUTHORIZED once Early Warning Signs are identified and why these are important to patient outcomes
NOTE: Patients hemodynamic status and assess airway, breathing and circulation by repeating VITAL SIGNS at least every 15 minutes.

Explain why it is necessary to ensure that the following items are ready / accessible:
    • Crash cart
    • Suction equipment
    • Oxygen delivery
    • IV set up and fluids
    • Dynamap with oxygen saturation probe
Define shock i.e. when cells become hypoxic as a result of decreased perfusion.

Discuss the categories and causes of shock:
Hypovolemic – massive external bleeding, hemothorax, fractures, gastrointestinal bleeding, diabetes mellitus insipidus burns, excessive diuretic use, ascites, massive vomiting or diarrhoea
Cardiogenic – MI, cardiomyopathy, cardiac contusion, dysrhythmias, heart valve disease
Distributive – sepsis, anaphylaxis, spinal cord injury, overdose, anoxia
Obstructive – tension pneumothorax, pericardial tamponade, pulmonary embolus, intra-cardiac clot, vena cava clot, aortic aneurysm, aortic stenosis, valvular disease, gravid uterus

Explore the cellular effects of shock e.g. < ATP (adenosine triphosphate), excess lactic acid production, mitochondrial death, cellular oedema, deterioration of the sodium-potassium pump, hyperkalaemia.

Discuss the progression of shock:
    • Compensatory – body responses initiated to increase cardiac output, tissue (cellular perfusion) and vital organ perfusion
    • Progressive – body responses become inadequate to maintain perfusion and multisystem failure ensues
    • Irreversible – pervasive cellular destruction; death is imminent

Explain the rationale for pertinent historical date:
    1. Chief Complaint
    2. Pain, pressure (PQRST)
        • Provocation
        • Quality
        • Radiation/region
        • Severity (scale 0-5 or 0-10)
        • Time of onset
    3. Level of consciousness
    4. Dizziness, syncope
    5. Weakness, fatigue
    6. Difficulty breathing
    7. Edema – location and type
    8. Vomiting, hematemesis
    9. Diarrhea, melena
    10. Vaginal bleeding
    11. Fever, chills
    12. Rash, urticarial
    13. Polyuria, thirst
    14. Injury, location, mechanism, force, protective device
    15. Bleeding, site, estimated blood loss
    16. Medical-surgical history
    17. Allergies

Discuss the acid base deviations that occur:
Respiratory Acidosis – Hypoventilation results in CO2 retention, carbonic acid excess and <pH
Metabolic Acidosis – Excess fixed acids results in <pH
Respiratory Alkalosis – Hyperventilation results in >CO2 exhaled, reducing carbonic acid with >pH
Metabolic Alkalosis – >pH due to excess base or acid deficits

Explore the adverse effects of fluid and/or blood replacement:
    1. Hypothermia – transfusion of banked blood without warming can make the patient hypothermic. Hypothermia shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the left i.e. oxygen is not available for the cells.
    2. Hyperkalemia – lysis of blood cells releases potassium from the intracellular space so the patient becomes hyperkalemic. Monitor the patient's serum potassium and observe for cardiac rhythm problems.
    3. Hypocalcaemia – banked blood contains citrate which binds with free calcium. Calcium chloride is given after 10U of blood.
    4. Acidosis – the pH of banked blood is 7.1 and with large amounts of banked blood, acidosis can occur. Monitor ABGs and watch for dysrhythmias.
    5. Alkalosis – large amounts of banked blood, alkalosis can develop because the citrate is converted by the liver into bicarbonate.
    6. Clotting problems – clotting factors are lost in most banked blood. Coagulation times may be prolonged and clotting problems occur with massive blood transfusions. Usually 1U of fresh-frozen plasma is given after 10U of blood.
    7. Intravascular debris – banked blood contains debris as a result of processing and therefore blood is always given through a filter.

Demonstrate the patient assessment for Stage 1 of shock:

Stage I – Compensatory
Increased heart rate (101-150 bpm)
Skin: pale, moist, clammy
Pupils: dilated (6-8 mm, react to light appropriately)
Blood pressure: usually normal at this stage
Heart rhythm: sinus tachycardia
Respirations: increased (>24 bpm)
Peripheral pulse: weak
Altered level of consciousness: confused, anxious, restless, lethargic
Glasgow Coma Scale
Poor capillary refill (>2 seconds)
May have petechiae or purpura
Depending on the cause may be at risk for infection
*This is the stage with the best chance of reversibility

Demonstrate the patient assessment for Stage 2 of shock:

Stage II – Progressive
Increased heart rate
Skin: cool, moist, clammy
Pupils: dilated, sluggish response
Blood pressure: starting to drop
Heart rhythm: sinus tachycardia
Respirations: rapid and deep
Altered level of consciousness worsens
Decreased urinary output
Peripheral edema
Dysrhythmias

Demonstrate the patient assessment for Stage 3 of shock:

Stage III - Irreversible
Decreased heart rate
Skin: cold
Pupils: dilated, very sluggish
Severe hypotension
Severe bradycardia
Respiratory failure
Possible coma
Anuria
Peripheral edema
Death
Demonstrate appropriate action when readings and vital signs and patient respiratory assessment findings are abnormal including the documentation of findings and action taken.
Complete the documentation for clinical management and patient assessment in the patient forms and notes according to area of practice.
attitude: Accept constrictive criticism as learning opportunity.
To be self-aware of limitation in knowledge and skills.
To be approachable and open to answer patient and family's questions and ability to educate both patient and family how to keep any IV lines etc. secure and in place.
Attentive to overall patient experience e.g. pain, anxiety and have ability to provide comfort and emotional support as needed.

Ability to organize and facilitate a Reflection session in and on practice after a MANAGEMENT AND CARE OF SHOCK learning opportunity occurs and activate findings to improve future practice and response.
